front: Visual metaphor: IPC is like workers in a toy shop working together. Give the three ways they interact and the matching process mechanism.
back:
• Share the work areas (leave common parts and tools on the table): processes share a portion of physical memory.
  • Call each other (explicit request and response): processes exchange messages via message passing APIs such as sockets.
  • Synchronize ("I will start a step once you finish yours"): processes wait on one another using a synchronization mechanism such as mutexes.

front: IPC: what does inter-process communication refer to?
back: A set of mechanisms the OS must support to permit multiple processes to interact with each other, including synchronization, coordination, and communication.

front: IPC: what are the two broad categories of IPC mechanisms, and which mechanisms belong to each?
back:
• Message-based: sockets, pipes, message queues.
  • Memory-based: shared memory, as unstructured shared physical memory pages or memory-mapped files.

front: IPC: how can files be seen as an IPC method?
back: Multiple processes can read and write the same file. (File systems are covered in a separate lecture.)

front: IPC: what is RPC and how does it differ from a plain communication channel?
back: Remote procedure calls provide higher-level IPC semantics. RPC is more than a channel for passing information: it also specifies the protocol(s) used, including the data format and the data exchange procedure.

front: IPC: why do synchronization primitives also count as IPC mechanisms?
back: Communication and coordination imply synchronization: processes that send and receive messages in a way synchronize, and processes that synchronize (e.g. with a mutex-like structure) communicate something about the point they have reached in their execution.

front: Message-based IPC: what is the OS responsible for, and what do processes do?
back: Processes create messages and send/receive them. The OS is responsible for creating and maintaining the channel used to send those messages. The channel can be thought of as a buffer or FIFO queue.

front: Message-based IPC: how do processes interact with the channel (ports)?
back: The OS provides an interface so processes can send messages via the channel. Processes send/write messages to a port and recv/read messages from a port; the channel passes the message from one port to the other.

front: Message-based IPC: what does every send and every receive call require, and why?
back: Each send and receive requires a system call and a data copy, because the OS must establish the communication and perform each IPC operation. On send, data is copied from the process address space into the channel; on receive, from the channel into the process address space.

front: Message-based IPC: how many user/kernel crossings and data copies does a request-response interaction between two processes require?
back: A total of four user/kernel crossings and four data copying operations. These overheads are one of the negatives of message-based IPC.

front: Message-based IPC: what does the lecture mean by its 'relative simplicity'?
back: Relative simplicity: the OS kernel takes care of all channel management and synchronization operations. It makes sure data is not overwritten or corrupted as processes send or receive it, potentially at the same time.

front: Forms of message passing: which form is the simplest, and what standard is it part of?
back: Pipes are the simplest form of message passing and are part of the POSIX standard.

front: Pipes: how many endpoints/processes, and is there a notion of a message?
back: Pipes have two endpoints, so only two processes can communicate. There is no notion of a message; just a stream of bytes pushed in by one process and read by the other.

front: Pipes: give a popular use of pipes.
back: Connecting the output of one process to the input of another, e.g. cat /some/really/large/file | grep "needle in a haystack" where | is the pipe operator.

front: Message queues: how do they differ from pipes in what they handle?
back: Message queues understand the notion of messages they can deliver. A sender must submit a properly formatted message to the channel, and the channel then delivers it to the receiving process.

front: Message queues: what OS-level functionality do they provide, and which APIs support them in Unix?
back: OS-level functionality includes message priority, custom message scheduling, and more. Two common APIs are SysV and POSIX.

front: Sockets: what operations does the socket API support and what do they do?
back: The socket is the OS-supported abstraction for ports. The API supports send and recv, which let processes move message buffers in and out of the kernel-level communication buffer.

front: Sockets: what does the socket call itself create and associate?
back: It creates a kernel-level socket buffer and associates any kernel-level processing needed with the socket plus the actual message movement. For a TCP/IP socket, the entire TCP/IP protocol stack is associated with the socket buffer.

front: Sockets: can communication cross machines, and what is the buffer between in that case?
back: Yes, socket-based communication can happen between processes on different machines. When the processes are on different machines, the communication buffer is really between the process and the network device that sends the data.

front: Sockets: what optimization happens when both processes are on the same machine?
back: The OS is smart enough to skip most of the protocol stack rather than send data onto the network only to receive it back. This stays hidden from the programmer, though it can be detected through performance measurements.

front: Shared memory IPC: what does the OS do, and must the virtual addresses match across processes?
back: The OS maps certain physical pages into the virtual address spaces of both processes. The virtual addresses pointing to a shared physical location do not have to be the same in each process, and the shared physical memory section need not be contiguous.

front: Shared memory IPC: are data copies avoided? What must happen for data to be shared?
back: Data copies are reduced but not necessarily avoided. Data must be explicitly allocated from the virtual addresses belonging to the shared memory region; otherwise it must be copied in and out of the shared region. If a process only needs to read arguments another left in the region, it can operate on them in place rather than copy them first.

front: Shared memory IPC: which protocol-related work falls to the developer, besides synchronization?
back: Processes must explicitly synchronize their shared memory operations since the region is concurrently accessible, and the developer must handle any protocol-related implementation: message format, delimiting, headers, and buffer allocation (when each process can use a portion of the buffer). This adds complexity to the application.

front: Shared memory IPC: which APIs do Unix systems support, and what other mechanisms can establish it?
back: Unix supports SysV and POSIX shared memory APIs. Shared memory IPC can also be established via a memory-mapped file (API essentially analogous to POSIX shared memory). Android uses a different form called Ashmem (mentioned only as a reference).

front: Copy vs. map: what is the shared goal of message-based and memory-based IPC?
back: To transfer data from the address space of one process to the address space of another process.

front: Copy vs. map: where are CPU cycles spent in each approach?
back:
• Message-based: CPU copies the data; cycles are spent every time data is copied to/from ports.
  • Memory-based: CPU cycles map physical memory into the address spaces; the CPU may also copy data into the shared space, but there is no user/kernel switching.

front: Copy vs. map: why can mapping beat copying even for one-time use?
back: When moving large amounts of data from one address space to another, the CPU time to copy via message-based IPC can greatly exceed the CPU time of the map operation performed in memory-based IPC.

front: Copy vs. map: how do Windows Local Procedure Calls (LPC) choose between copy and map?
back: If the data is smaller than a threshold, it is copied in and out of a channel via a port-like interface. Otherwise it is copied once into a page-aligned area that is then mapped into the target process's address space.

text: The Windows mechanism that copies small data via a port-like interface but maps large page-aligned data into the target address space is called {{c1::Local Procedure Calls}} (LPC).

front: SysV shared memory: what is a segment, and must it be contiguous physical pages?
back: The unit in which the SysV OS supports shared memory. A segment does not need to correspond to contiguous physical pages.

front: SysV shared memory: how does the OS treat shared memory, and what limits result?
back: As a shared resource governed by system-wide policies, so there is a limit on the total number of segments and the total size of shared memory. Currently in Linux the limit is 4000 segments; in the past it was much lower: as few as 6 in certain OSs, and 128 in more recent (but not current) Linux versions.

front: SysV shared memory: when a segment is created, what does the OS allocate and assign?
back: It allocates the required amount of physical memory and assigns the segment a unique key that identifies it within the OS; another process can refer to the segment using that key.

front: SysV shared memory: how do other processes learn the key to communicate via a segment?
back: The creating process must make sure the others learn the key somehow, for example via some other form of IPC, by passing it through a file, or as a command line argument.

front: SysV shared memory: what does attaching a segment mean, and can multiple processes attach?
back: The OS establishes a valid mapping between the process's virtual addresses and the physical addresses backing the segment. Multiple processes can attach; reads and writes are visible across all attached processes.

front: SysV shared memory: what does detaching a segment do?
back: It invalidates the virtual address mappings for the virtual address region that corresponded to the segment in that process; the page table entries for those addresses are no longer valid.

front: SysV shared memory: is a segment destroyed when detached? What is its lifetime?
back: No. A segment can be attached, detached, and re-attached many times. Once created it is a persistent entity until an explicit destroy request or a system reboot, similar to a file that persists until explicitly deleted, and unlike process-local memory, which is reclaimed when the process exits.

front: SysV API: what call creates or opens a segment, and what are its arguments?
back: shmget(shmid, size, flag): size sets the segment size and flag sets flags such as permissions.

front: SysV API: who creates the shmid key, and what call generates it?
back: The key is not created by the OS; the application passes it in. ftok(pathname, proj_id) generates the token.

front: SysV API: how does ftok let different processes agree on the same key?
back: ftok is basically a hashing function: the same arguments always yield the same key, so different processes can independently obtain the same unique key for the segment they want to share.

front: SysV API: what call attaches a segment, and what does passing NULL for addr do?
back: shmat(shmid, addr, flags). The programmer may supply the virtual addresses via addr; passing NULL lets the OS choose suitable addresses.

front: SysV API: what must the programmer do with the virtual address returned by shmat?
back: Cast the returned address to the appropriate type, since it can be interpreted in various ways; this is the programmer's responsibility.

front: SysV API: what call detaches a segment and what does it do?
back: shmdt(shmid), which invalidates the virtual-to-physical mappings associated with the shared segment.

front: SysV API: what call sends commands about a segment, and how do you destroy a segment?
back: shmctl(shmid, cmd, buf). Specifying IPC_RMID as cmd destroys the segment.

text: In the SysV shared memory API: {{c1::shmget}} creates/opens a segment, {{c2::shmat}} attaches it, {{c3::shmdt}} detaches it, and {{c4::shmctl}} sends control commands.

front: POSIX shared memory: what does it use instead of segments, and since when is it supported on Linux?
back: It uses files instead of segments. Supported on Linux since the 2.4 kernel, and despite being the standard it is not as widely supported as the SysV API.

front: POSIX shared memory: are these real filesystem files? Where do they live?
back: No. They are not real files used elsewhere by the OS; they live in the tmpfs filesystem, which looks and feels like a filesystem but is really just state in physical memory. The OS reuses its file data structures to represent pages of a shared memory region.

front: POSIX shared memory: why is there no key generation process?
back: Because shared memory regions are now referenced by a file descriptor, there is no longer a need for key generation.

front: POSIX shared memory: name the calls to create/open, attach, detach, remove the fd, and delete the segment.
back:
• Create/open: shm_open (regular open and close also work, since it is a file)
  • Attach: mmap
  • Detach: munmap
  • Remove fd from process only: the regular close on the file descriptor (the lecture's "shared memory close"; POSIX has no shm_close)
  • Delete data structures and free segment: shm_unlink

front: POSIX shared memory: what is the difference between closing the region (the lecture's "shared memory close") and shm_unlink?
back: Closing (the regular close on the file descriptor; POSIX has no shm_close) only removes the file descriptor from the process. To actually delete the shared memory data structures and free the segment you must call shm_unlink.

front: Shared memory and sync: why must shared memory accesses be synchronized?
back: Because data in shared memory can be concurrently accessed by all processes with access, so accesses must be synchronized to avoid race conditions, the same situation as in multithreaded environments.

front: Shared memory and sync: what are the two options for handling inter-process synchronization?
back:
• Use mechanisms supported by threading libraries (e.g. two pthreads processes using pthreads mutexes and condition variables).
  • Use OS-provided mechanisms for synchronization available for IPC.

front: Shared memory and sync: what two kinds of coordination must any chosen mechanism provide?
back:
• Coordinate the number of concurrent accesses to shared segments (think mutexes).
  • Coordinate communicating when data is available or ready for consumption (think condition variables and signals).

front: PThreads sync for IPC: what attribute makes a mutex or condition variable shared across processes?
back: PTHREAD_PROCESS_SHARED, specified in the attribute structs passed to mutex/condition variable initialization, ensures the sync variables are visible across processes.

front: PThreads sync for IPC: where must a PTHREAD_PROCESS_SHARED mutex/condition variable itself be allocated?
back: In shared memory: the synchronization data structures must themselves live in the shared region.

front: PThreads sync for IPC: how is the segment identifier created and passed in the example?
back: Create the identifier with ftok, passing argv[0] (the pathname for the program executable) and an integer parameter (120 in the example), then pass that id into shmget with a segment size of 1KB plus flags.

front: PThreads sync for IPC: in the example, what two fields does the shared struct (shm_data_struct_t) hold?
back: The actual buffer of information (the data) and a mutex that controls access to the data. The attached address from shmat is cast to this struct type.

front: PThreads sync for IPC: what are the steps to create a process-shared mutex in the example?
back:
1. Create the mutexattr struct.
  2. Set its pshared attribute with PTHREAD_PROCESS_SHARED.
  3. Initialize the mutex with that struct, using the pointer to the mutex inside the struct that lives in shared memory.

front: PThreads sync for IPC: how are process-shared condition variables set up, and how does using them differ from regular ones?
back: With a similar set of operations as for the mutex (attribute struct with PTHREAD_PROCESS_SHARED, object in shared memory). Once created, process-shared mutexes and condition variables are used exactly like regular ones in a multithreaded pthreads process; there is no difference in usage.

front: Sync for other IPC: why rely on OS-provided sync mechanisms instead of PTHREAD_PROCESS_SHARED?
back: Because PTHREAD_PROCESS_SHARED is not necessarily supported on every platform, so other means such as message queues and semaphores are used.

front: Sync for other IPC: how can message queues implement mutual exclusion (give the A/B example)?
back: Via send/recv: process A writes data to shared memory then sends a "ready" message into the queue; process B receives the message, reads the data, and sends an "ok" message back.

front: Sync for other IPC: how do the SysV message queue and semaphore APIs relate to the SysV shared memory API?
back: They are similar in form to the SysV shared memory API in how constructs are created, controlled, and closed, and POSIX equivalents exist for both.

front: Sync for other IPC: name the four SysV message queue system calls on Linux and what each does.
back:
• msgsnd: send a message.
  • msgrcv: receive a message.
  • msgctl: perform a control operation.
  • msgget: obtain a message queue identifier.

front: IPC command line tools: what does ipcs do, and what does the -m flag restrict it to?
back: ipcs lists all IPC facilities in the system across all IPC types (including message queues and semaphores); passing -m restricts output to shared memory.

front: IPC command line tools: what does ipcrm do, and how do you remove a shared memory segment with it?
back: ipcrm removes an IPC construct; use -m with a shared memory identifier to remove a shared memory segment.

front: Design considerations: with shared memory, who decides how the memory is used and how data passing and synchronization work?
back: The programmer. The OS does not restrict how the memory is used: it provides the shared area and then is out of the way, so beyond choosing the API and sync mechanism, all data passing and synchronization protocols are up to the programmer.

front: Design considerations: one large shared segment vs multiple segments, what does each require?
back:
• One large segment: you must implement management of the shared memory, i.e. a manager that allocates and frees memory in the region.
  • Multiple segments (one per pairwise communication): pre-allocate a pool ahead of time and manage how segments are picked up, e.g. a queue of segment ids.

front: Design considerations: why pre-allocate a pool of segments when using one segment per pairwise communication?
back: So you do not incur the cost of creating a segment in the middle of execution.

front: Design considerations: with a pool of segments, how does a thread tell its peer which segment it will use?
back: A thread does not know up front which segment it will use, so if that matters it can communicate the chosen segment id to the peer through another mechanism such as a message queue.

front: Design considerations: when can you simply make all segments one fixed size, and why is that limited?
back:
When the data size is known up front and static; then fixed-size segments work well. Two problems:
  • data sizes may be dynamic, not static
  • it limits the maximum data transferable, because the OS typically imposes a maximum segment size

front: Design considerations: how do you support arbitrary message sizes larger than the segment size?
back: Transfer the data in rounds: the sender sends the message in chunks and the receiver reads and saves them until the whole message arrives. The programmer needs a protocol to track progress, and the shared area is typically cast as a data structure holding the data buffer, a synchronization construct, and progress-tracking flags.
